paragraphs.heading: A crowd of galaxies
paragraphs.text: The Virgo Cluster is a big gathering of galaxies whose center lies about 53.8 million light-years from us, in the direction of the constellation Virgo. It counts roughly 1,300 member galaxies, and perhaps as many as 2,000. On the sky it spreads over a patch about 8 degrees across. It sits at the heart of a still larger structure, the Virgo Supercluster, and our own Local Group, home of the Milky Way, is part of that supercluster.

paragraphs.heading: Very heavy, very fast
paragraphs.text: The cluster is very massive: estimates put its mass at 1.2×10¹⁵ M_(☉) within a radius of about 2.2 Mpc of its center. One sign of all that mass is speed, since many of its galaxies move very fast relative to the center, sometimes as fast as 1,600 km/s. Its gravity also slows the galaxies around it. Our Local Group is still moving away from the cluster, but about ten percent more slowly because of that pull. We feel the mass of the wider supercluster as what is called the Virgocentric flow.

paragraphs.heading: Old fuzzy patches in the sky
paragraphs.text: Many of its brighter galaxies were found in the late 1770s and early 1780s and went into Charles Messier's catalogue of fuzzy objects that were not comets. Messier called them nebulae without stars, and what they really were stayed unknown until the 1920s. One of them is the giant elliptical galaxy M87, whose central supermassive black hole had its event horizon observed by the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration in 2019. The cluster's brightest member, though, is another elliptical, Messier 49. Some of the leading members show up in binoculars or small telescopes, and a 6-inch telescope can pick out about 160 of its galaxies on a clear night.

paragraphs.heading: Spirals and ellipticals
paragraphs.text: The members are a fairly mixed set of spiral and elliptical galaxies. The ellipticals are packed more toward the center than the spirals are. As of 2004, the spirals were thought to lie along a stretched-out filament, about four times as long as it is wide, pointing along our line of sight. The cluster's core is also where the first ultra-diffuse galaxy was found, in 1984. Fainter members, especially the many dwarf galaxies, usually go by their numbers in the Virgo Cluster Catalog.

paragraphs.heading: Hot gas between the galaxies
paragraphs.text: Like many other rich clusters, Virgo is filled with a thin, hot plasma, at about 30 million kelvins, that gives off X-rays; this is the intracluster medium. Pressure from this dense medium strips molecular gas out of many of the cluster's galaxies, a process called ram pressure stripping. Losing that gas can in time shut down star formation in those galaxies. The intracluster medium also holds many stars that belong to no galaxy, up to 10% of the cluster's stars, which may have been thrown out of their home galaxies by encounters with other galaxies. It even holds some globular clusters and at least one region where stars are forming.
